posts.author: Joe Farina
posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
Since the options for a blue laser (for holography) are very limited (to say the least) Colin's post about Analog Technologies caught my attention. They have (?) a 50mW 405nm laser for a good price.

Does anyone care to speculate about a 405nm laser for three-wavelength color holography? That is, a HeNe for the red, a DPSS for the green, and this one for the blue. According to Kaveh, it's best to stay at 477nm (argon) or below. This would probably mean a "5 watt" (or greater) type of argon (water cooled and probably three-phase) with an etalon (to get a reasonable amount of power at 477, i.e., 50mW). A lot of expense and hassle in that case.

The only other option I know of is the Melles Griot DPSS lasers (the ones having the long coherence length option) at 457 and 473. Last time I checked the 100mW (long coherence model) 457 laser cost $19,000 new.

If 405nm works, the price tag on the Analog Technologies laser ($3,150) looks a lot better. (Assuming the laser works and they are able to deliver!)

posts.content_md:
Colin, I don't know about the price of the Coherent laser you mentioned. Are you sure it has a coherence length suitable for holography? If it does, then I'm fairly certain it's way out of my price range, since it would be the equivalent of the Melles Griot laser I mentioned (assuming it has similar power).

I looked at the 1976 C.I.E. diagram, and I assume 405nm corresponds to the "lowest" point (i.e., the bottom corner) since it's right at the limit of visible light. (Is that correct?) If so, then I would think that the range of colors which could be produced would be quite large (supposedly, those colors lying within the triangle formed by 405 to 532 to 633 are reproducable). However, as Kaveh has pointed out very clearly, it's not the size of the triangle that really matters. He has also stated that the optimal wavelengths are those near 450, 540, and 610. I saw a color hologram in Lake Forest that was made with HeCd at 442, and that wavelength works well. The question is, what effect would 405 have as opposed to 442-477?

posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
If you expose with 405, 532 and 633, then post-swell the hologram by (let's say) 30nm, you'd end up with 435, 562 and 660. Those wavelengths look pretty good. I don't know if the three colors of the image would stay together, but if you can find a 405nm laser easily ( and most importantly, cheap!), I'd go for it.

I'm currently using 473, 532 and 633. The 473nm laser is the 30mW version described here: [http://www.intelite.com/bluesys.htm](http://www.intelite.com/bluesys.htm). The coherence length as delivered is not good for pictorial work, but the laser came to me easily so that's what I'm using.

posts.topic_title: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md: There's a vast range of different wavelengths possible and these "gamut wars" have been going on for quite a while. If you look at the work of Paul Hubel , you'll see a totally differrent gamut. Each side has their own reasons for their favorite gamut. As Bob says, you can always swell anyway. Obviously the greater the gamut, the greater the range of wavelengths. There are also other factors involved. Recently I've discovered that it's not just the gamut per se. The impression of color is very different from the inclusion of color - radiometric vs photometric. The impression of color we sense is not just the radiometric combination of a specific set of wavelengths, but the inclusion of weighting factors on the photopic curve. I'm now beginning to believe there's probably not any specific "ideal gamut" at all. I think we need to get away from the whole RGB color space. To add further to the confusion, there are recent papers that seem to indiocate that any gamut must consist of more than just rgb, but must involve 4 or more. The idea being that a polygon is more representative than a triangle.

posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
As to the question of 3 wavelengths versus 4, you can see what's possible with 3 in the work of Gentet. He uses 633, 532, and 476.5. As far as I'm concerned, that's the end of the story.

Even three lasers aren't needed for the moment, since no one seems to have adequately explored the possibilities of using two. So it's not necessary to have a battery of high-power, etalon-equipped argons or kryptons.

I have enough papers on color holography to make anyone's head spin. At some point, the papers must be put aside (sometimes I think they should be thrown away) and work must begin in earnest. If someone wants to make color holograms, they should get two lasers, provide themselves with adequate lab space, and start work. This alone can be quite enough of a challenge for some people (myself included).

posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
> **Dinesh:** There's a vast range of different wavelengths possible and these "gamut wars" have been going on for quite a while.

Love it: Gamut wars!!

I am worried that 405nm might be too short, just because it is on the limit of the sensitivity of the eye. Think of it this way. To get the maximum gamut, you can use the deepest blue that the eye can see. But the eye can only just see it, so it will be very dim. So you have to come in a bit, i.e. increase the wavelength, so you can see the damn thing!!

I think people have complicated the subject too much. If you don't have the perfect set of wavelengths, it just means you'll get some distortion in the colours. Yellows will appear brown or pink, blues might be the wrong shade, etc. But you will get a colour hologram for sure. So go for it, with the caveat that 405 might be too dark to see.

And yes, you can use two wavelengths only. In fact you would start that way to begin with. The result will be surprisingly good. The eye will fill in the missing colours.

I also have difficulty in understanding some of the papers on colour holography. I tried to figure out Paul Hubel's papers, but too many integrals!!

posts.topic_title: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.author: BobH
posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
In my opinion, any discussion of multi-wavelength "full color" holography (as opposed to simply "color" holography ... they're not black & white) regarding which wavelengths to use, saturation or color rendering is moot unless the final hologram is installed in a display with a known reconstruction source and geometry. Furthermore, the hologram would need to be produced for that display only, and tuned for the source used.

I believe the general public sees *all* holograms as "color" holograms, and that for some reason the holographer chose a single color to render their subject. Again, nobody makes black & white holograms! I think this is part of why holograms are not very well accepted. The colors available (mostly burnt orange, jaundiced yellow, pea green, and dark green) are not very appealing. 

Arguments about color gamut and pictorial holography are missing the forest for the trees. And speaking of trees, I made a hologram of a cannabis plant a while ago, using 

a) Ron Olson's pulsed green laser for the master, 

b) a He-Ne to make a ganged inter-master (by pre-swelling with TEA) which reconstructed at 514nm, and

c) an Argon Ion laser for production in Dupont's photopolymer.

The final photopolymer holograms (and the hand made copies made by me in AgX with the He-Ne) are very close to the color of the original subject. This is an example of a "full color" hologram made with a single wavelength (the different wavelengths used are academic, the image could have been produced all the way through with 532nm). 

This example contradicts my opinion above only because the "green" of the image can vary quite a bit and still represent the subject acceptably. When a scene requireing the full spectrum is contemplated, I think the "reconstruction" part of wavefront reconstruction must be incorporated into the discussion.

posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
[quote:07d77bbdf2="BobH"]

I believe the general public sees [i:07d77bbdf2]all[/i:07d77bbdf2] holograms as "color" holograms, and that for some reason the holographer chose a single color to render their subject. Again, nobody makes black & white holograms! I think this is part of why holograms are not very well accepted. The colors available (mostly burnt orange, jaundiced yellow, pea green, and dark green) are not very appealing. [/quote:07d77bbdf2]

I think this question of why holograms are not well accepted is a perennial question in holography. The problem as I see it is that the public (and holographers!) don't see a role for holography in the public eye. Image construction and reconstruction are based on some sense of utility as well as aesthetics and each method of image reconstruction is based on some ratio of these two. I think both we and the public tend not to notice this. If someone were to ask, "Do you like photographs?" I would imagine the question to be meaningless because it has no context. On the other hand we make these blanket statements about holography as if it should be judged by and of itself with no contextual background. 

I think monochromatic holograms do have a role, but not simply to hang on a wall and admired just for themselves. Similarly "full colour" holograms have a different role and also not just to be hung on a wall. When we say the public has not accepted holography we tend to forget that they've accepted it perfectly well on credit cards, on magazine covers, postage stamps and even wrapping paper. However, many holographers tend to scoff and say, "Well they're not real holograms, they're dot matrix/mass produced/security or some such dismissive term. We tend to see a glass plate (usually dark) with some object or objects in it in garish colour(s) and think of that as a real hologram. We then rack our minds and go head-to-head about making it more real/less real/more abstract etc etc and wonder why the public don't like this. It seems to me that without context a glass plate with a cat or a plant or a dolphin or even a miniature dinosaur is simply that. 

If a hologram is to factually and identically convey visual impressions and information, I feel it needs to do so in some context where such a representation is required - a print ad or a book illustration eg. If the hologram is to convey the essence of some visual object without complete factual information - a green dolphin eg - then it may be appropriate in some context but not in the standard context of any pictorial representation the public is familiar with. Certainly no one would buy a green dolphin just to hang on a wall and impress their friends. If the intent is to do just this, it needs to have the whole culture of pictorial art embedded somehow in it. A green dolphin or multicoloured butterflies ain't Picasso!

posts.topic_title: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
I've always wondered why you don't see more achromats in embossed holograms. After all, you can shoot an achromat onto resist just as easily as a rainbow and electroplate it. The average spatial frequency is about the same. Jason Sappan did a very stunning one for a magazine cover where you had a white (achromat) image against a rainbow background. But in general, you tend not to see that many achromats. We made a small (2.5in x 2.5in achromat folded into a small box. When opened, the achromat hologram would fold open and lock into place, like those old travelling clocks, with a blue LED behind it.

[quote:b979422cf8]What about three color transmission holography! That could be really stunning.[/quote:b979422cf8]

I've thought about this a lot, but can't figure out how you'd distinguish colour information. If you had a red object next to a green object and back lit them both with an rgb combination of LEDs, how would the red object only diffract the red LED and not the green? How would you record them as an achromat ? Any achromat (open aperture) recording geometry would simply record them as white. I thought of different ref angles (relying on Bragg selectivity) but just ended up with two white objects at different angles. I know that years ago Kaveh was playing with an idea of a super thick emulsion that was not available back then. I've had thoughts along similar lines with DCG. I've even toyed with the idea of edge lit from three different edges.

Watch this space!

I have always stated, I too prefer achromatic holograms over the green or red mono-colored ones. It is what I have always shot for in DCG. My reason being very simply that the general public is used to a black and white (photograph) as oposed to a black and green (photograph), even if the subject is supposed to be green. It simple does not have a natural green, it's mono. Let's face it, a lot of persons still remember black and white TV and photographs. In fact the home developer and schools that teach photography and developing teach it in black and white. A black and white image of a figurine looks more natural then an all green figurine.

> **Dinesh:** If someone were to ask, "Do you like photographs?" I would imagine the question to be meaningless because it has no context.
 I have to completely disagee on this subject. Some may say it is meaningless but ask a person that avidly takes photographs and you may find a different answer, especially one of the thousands of professional photographers. Ask a woman who has just got married. Ask a person who has just lost a loved one. Ask an editor to a glamour magazine. I think my point is made. When I was growing up I got my first 35mm camera at age 9. I never put is down and I took photographs of everything. It was not simple the subject that I loved but the actual recoding of an image. I used to used fish eye lenses, double exposures, filters, all to make the photograph unusual, not so much the subject. So I think there is the group that will not understand the question as you have stated but there is a very large number of persons that you can not negate that will simply state they love photographs and photography.

posts.topic_title: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.author: Dinesh
posts.post_subject: Blue laser for color holography/Analog Technologies?
posts.content_md:
I think you may have missed the point. Of course, everyone likes photographs. However, it's always a specific kind of photograph, not a general lumping of all photographs. It seems it's pretty true of almost anything. Perhaps I could phrase the question: "Do you like food?" Of course everyone likes some kind of food, but the question as posed is meaningless. I, for example, like photographs of outdoor panoramas if done well. However tourist photos of "Our Hotel" or "The Ski Slope" have value only to the family and some friends of the photographer. We're all aware of how boring it can be to see someone's holiday snaps or pictures of Mickey on "The Trip To California".

My point was that, just like photographs, holograms need context. I think it's impossible to just "like" or "not like" holograms. I'm pretty indifferent to holograms of routine single objects, be they dolphins or glass bottles. Just the fact that you can make a hologram of a dolphin or glass bottle in orange/blue or orange and blue is pretty "bleah!". However, I like Dan Scweitzer's work a lot, also Rudy Berkhout. I liked Lon Moore's pseudocoloured rocks when I first saw them. However, my attempts at pseusdocolour back in the 80's were bleah! (except to me, of course!). Peter Miller did some pretty stuinning work on pseudocolour. I like the way Tom B presents the subject matter. Just like photographs, you can't just "like holograms". I think it's pretty similar to the public at large. They're not impressed with glass bottles in orange or multicoloured butterflies or green dolphins because to the public, this is very simuilar to "Little Denise posing with Goofy with the Disney castle in the background" It's awfully sweet to the parents of Little Denise and awfully bleah! to the rest of us! The public needs context or cultural value. A pink flamingo singing Elvis has cultural value (to some!) but a hologram of a pink flamingo has none,except to the holographer, his/her friends and family and to those who think every hologram is stupendous! wonderful! amazing! If holographers think this, I think they need to realise that not everyone does. There are holographers who've achieved some technical feat or done something in a non-standard way. This may, or may not impress other holographers, but then to say "Why don't the public like holograms?" when you parade a hologram in orange or bright colours or made with soda cans or that faithfully represent this or that colour is simply meaningless to them. Lenticulars come very, very large and in 3D. OK, there's no parallax, but there's colour, size and depth. Our main competition has nothing to do with "3D" (an overhyped word these days, anyway) but our fascination with a medium irrespective of any cultural "hook"

By the way, by "achromat" I was not referring to broadband DCG but to the transmission format that creates a greyscale image in any medium. I actually don't agree that the general public likes (or even remembers!) black and white photos. Except in newspapers and some magazines, the general public doesn't see them anymore. I'm not sure of photography courses, however here in San Diego we have a photography exhibition every year. Usually there are about 500 or so photos from amateur to pro. There are no (or very few) black-and-whites submitted.
